Sabbat.et: From Middle High German sabbat, sābāot, sābot, from Latin sabbatum, from Ancient Greek σάββατον (sábbaton), from Hebrew שַׁבָּת (shabát, “Sabbath”).

Sabotage.et: Ca. 1900, unadapted borrowing from French sabotage. By surface analysis, sabotieren + -age.

Säbel.et: From Late Middle High German sabel, possibly from Old Polish szabla (cp. Polish szabla), from Hungarian szablya.

s: a female given name, a less common variant of Sabine
a female given name from English, popular from the 1970's to the 1990's

sabbern.et:
Borrowed from Low German and Middle Low German sabben, ultimately from the source of Saft (“juice, sap”).
Closely related to sabbeln (“to babble”). Compare southern Dutch zabberen and standard Dutch sabbelen.

s: a female given name, popular in Germany from the 1950's to the 1970's
Sabine.et: From the Latin saint's name Sabina.

S-Abf.et: Abbreviation of System-Abfrage, a calque of English system request.

s: jabber, gab, rattle on, rabbit on (to talk a lot and quickly, or to talk nonsense)
sabbeln.et:
Related to sabbern (“to drivel, drool”).
This word entered standard German alongside sabbern from Low German [Term?]. Subsequently, the meaning of this term shifted; sabbern retains the original meaning, "drool". Compare southern Dutch zabberen, standard Dutch…
